stories.title: Taoiseach to meet CUH officials amid staffing concerns
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin will meet Cork University Hospital officials today to discuss significant patient safety and staffing level concerns. However, Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill and HSE Chief Executive Anne O'Connor will not be in attendance. The meeting comes after significant national attention over patient safety and staffing levels at CUH. While the issues have been raised privately since late spring, CUH Chief Executive Jennifer Kearney warned the Government and the HSE of the situation and her concerns over the winter period in a letter in August. On 17 August, Ms Kearney wrote to the HSE's Integrated Healthcare Area Manager for the South and West, Priscilla Lynch, to make her aware of her "increasing concern" about patient safety risks at the hospital as winter approached. The subject line was marked "URGENT" and referenced "patient safety risk arising from employment approval processes".

stories.title: France and Germany to take key ECB roles
stories.summary: France has nominated economist Laurence Boone to the ECB's executive board, as Europe's most powerful financial institution reshuffles three of the most vital roles in quick succession. The European Central Bank is replacing its president, chief economist and the board member in charge of market operations, just as it fights high inflation and the prospect of renewed market turbulence triggered by French political turmoil. Boone is expected to take on the markets portfolio. This could land the Santander executive and former OECD chief economist at the centre of any financial storm, particularly if it spreads beyond France and forces ECB intervention. The announcement puts Spain's Pablo Hernandez de Cos on track to take over from President Christine Lagarde in February while Germany's Markus Brunnermeier, nominated earlier this week, is likely to be the ECB's next chief economist when Ireland's Philip Lane leaves on May 31. All nominations are subject to confirmation, which could still hit a snag as the reshuffle leaves the ECB's 27-member Governing Council with just one woman, since each of the euro zone's 21 national central banks is led by men and the board is also male-dominated. Only one woman, Chrystalla Georghadji of Cyprus, has ever served as a euro zone national central bank governor and only five women have served on the ECB's board.

stories.title: Ireland deliver reminder they can still mix with the best
stories.summary: Between the build-up, the performance and the emotional energy expended on Saturday, you nearly had to remind yourself that there's another game to be played this week. Granted, there's a slight anticlimactic feeling to the reward for beating the Springboks; a six-day turnaround for a fifth-place play-off against Australia at Twickenham, but it takes nothing away from what happened on Saturday. There is a lot of road to be travelled between now and the World Cup, and Ireland know only too well that their win counts for little if they can't back it up next year, but after two years of struggling to land a blow on the game's Big Three, they have reminded themselves they can still mix it with the best. And while they were considerable underdogs at home to the world champions, their head coach insists he had "a sense" there was a big performance coming. "These lads knew exactly what was coming. You get a feeling that it's a big week," Andy Farrell (below) said after Saturday's gripping win. "They're not normal Tuesdays or Wednesdays. We got that sense all week.

stories.title: Tin Castle - the new documentary exploring Traveller culture
stories.summary: Ahead of its release in Irish cinemas, filmmaker Alexander Murphy introduces Tin Castle, his acclaimed new documentary offering an intimate portrait of the Tipperary-based O'Reillys, a Traveller family of 12 living together in their mobile home, affectionately known as their 'tin castle’, along a country road. I've always felt a certain curiosity towards Traveller culture. I imagined a community of people who were free-spirited and deeply proud of their identity. Yet, the reality I encountered was quite different. Many Travellers feel compelled to hide their identity to integrate into wider society, and often live in difficult conditions. I met the O'Reilly family in 2020. They seemed to exist on the margins of everything: on the fringes of wider society, but also isolated from other Traveller communities. Their home was separated from the rest of the world by a motorway, a physical barrier that seemed to reflect their social isolation. There is a deep-rooted stigma surrounding the Traveller community. I knew that, if I wanted to capture their reality with honesty and build a bridge between the audience and the O'Reilly family, I would need to spend a lot of time with them. I needed to get to know them, gain their trust and allow their story to unfold naturally. At first, I went alone. I wanted them to get used to me and feel comfortable around me. Talking about vulnerability and emotions takes time, and sometimes it felt like we had to start again from scratch. Eventually, I spent some time living in the caravan next door. I decided to operate the camera and record sound myself, so that I wouldn't have a film crew around disturbing their everyday life. Gradually, I realised that the camera itself needed to become part of the family, almost like an eleventh child. I wanted the film to feel less like a documentary and more like a home movie, creating a sense of closeness, as if we, the audience, were part of the family too. Over a couple of years, I filmed the love within the O'Reilly family. At times, I even found myself a little jealous of it. I wanted to be part of that tribe. I don't know if I ever really managed to become part of it, but perhaps the camera did. I wanted to adopt the children's perspective because, through their eyes, we enter into their kingdom. There is no miserabilism in the way they see the world. I also wanted to avoid turning the film into a form of voyeurism. It was important to keep certain family secrets. Seeing things through the children's eyes allowed me to maintain a distance: a child can sense tensions within a family without necessarily understanding exactly what is going on. The O'Reillys live in a world balanced on a tightrope, between a culture they are trying to preserve and a world they are forced to adapt to. It has become increasingly difficult for Travellers to find work. Many have become more sedentary, often forced to settle in houses close to neighbours who regard them with hostility. With less space, they are also becoming disconnected from their animals. Horses remain at the very heart of Traveller life. At first, I thought I was filming a culture about to disappear. Over time, I realised I was capturing something very much alive, but constantly changing. There is a strange contradiction between the respect shown towards the culture and the rejection of the people who carry it. That paradox is both strange and troubling. I hope that, in its own way, Tin Castle can open up a dialogue and perhaps shift.

stories.title: Looking back at 21 years of the M50, as Galway takes on its own
stories.summary: It took 34 years – and protests, tribunals and a lot of headlines – for the M50 to be completed. Now that Galway is set to get their own, is history doomed to repeat itself? Kate Demolder writes. 21 years ago this June, the final section of the M50 motorway officially opened to traffic, closing Ireland's most chaotic, and generation-spanning engineering project. At 45.5km, and a structure that handles some 160,000 vehicles daily, the M50 is not just a road, but a permanent fixture in the Irish psyche. By the time the final tarmac was laid in 2005 – 34 years after it was first proposed, and 17 years after the first sod was turned – the M50 came to hold up a mirror to a rapidly changing Ireland: from fields worth fighting for to a monument to the growing pains of the Celtic Tiger. In more ways than one, the story behind it would make a great feature film. Originally planned against a background of economic stagnancy, the year was 1971 when Dublin’s planning authorities formally proposed a C-ring orbital route to divert heavy freight away from the city centre. Few believed it would actually go ahead.

stories.title: Pacific nations express dismay as no COP31 deal reached
stories.summary: Climate advocates have reacted with indignation to the COP31 summit ending in failure, with contentious talks collapsing over fossil fuels after the meeting in Turkey stretched into record overtime. The final agreement was rejected yesterday in a chaotic finale to the UN climate summit that ran two days over schedule, underscoring the strains on diplomacy in an increasingly fractured world. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, who urged nations to send fossil fuels "the way of the dinosaurs" during a fiery appearance at the talks, expressed deep dismay. "I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands," the outgoing UN chief said in a statement. Pacific island nations, which are facing rising sea levels and other existential threats from climate change, expressed deep disappointment. "We ‌have been let down on all sides," the delegation from the Marshall Islands at COP31 said in a statement.

stories.title: Kenmare Resources receives possible cash offer from IRH
stories.summary: Titanium and zircon miner Kenmare Resources said today that it has agreed a deal in principle with Abu-Dhabi-based International Resources Holdings on the financial terms of a pre-conditional possible cash offer for the company. The deal values the entire issued and to be issued share capital of Kenmare at about £352.8m. Kenmare said its board would be "unanimously minded" to recommend the deal. Under the terms of the deal, Kenmare shareholders would be entitled to receive 380 pence in cash per share. Kenmare operates the Moma Titanium Minerals Mine in northern Mozambique, and its products are used in such items as paints, plastics and ceramic tiles. The miner's shares had jumped over 20% on October 6 after it received a non-binding proposal from the Abu-Dhabi-based company regarding a possible cash offer.

stories.title: Brendan O'Connor on how fatherhood gave him 'massive clarity'
stories.summary: In Able, Brendan O'Connor meets six jobseekers with varying disabilities for an emotional TV show freighted with a personal resonance. Donal O’Donoghue talks to the broadcaster about ability, family matters and fatherhood. "This is a whole new type of thing for me," says Brendan O'Connor, of his upcoming TV series, Able, which chronicles the lives of six people with differing disabilities looking for work. In this scenario O’Connor is, as he puts it, not so much a presenter as simply being present: listening, encouraging, helping, outlining the big picture and tapping into the human details as we follow Alex, Conor, Emma, Kevin, Melissa and Niall on their odyssey. We also get a snapshot of O’Connor’s life: the self-confessed "bit of a show-off" from his early TV panellist, rapping 'priest’ days to his life as the parent, with Sarah, of two daughters, Anna and Mary, the latter who has Down syndrome. Of all he has done – print, TV, radio – Able, his first television in yonks, is probably the most personal, even though he had initial reservations. "I figured to best way to do it, as the producer suggested, was just show up and be there with them." Since then, he, and the show (O’Connor always stresses it’s a team effort, not a solo job), have bagged umpteen awards, including IMRO’s Moment of the Year (a raw, revealing interview with the late Brenda Fricker) in October. "I’ve become more a listener, being present, realising that less is always better," he says. "So, if I’m learning anything it’s just telling myself: ‘shut up! shut up! shut up!’". He also acknowledges the difficulties. "There’s no way of doing this perfectly," he says. "I do not have a disability and I’m not an expert in disability, but I said to the six participants at the beginning that I would be guided by them. But I still think that when it goes out, there will be people who will have issues with it, but the intentions here are really good. And while this show does not have all the answers by any stretch, it’s asking a few interesting questions that hopefully will nudge along the conversation." O’Connor, a master of the gentle nudge ("come here and tell me"), is also nudged in unexpected ways in a TV series that is, at times, an emotional rollercoaster for its six jobseekers and its presenter too. "Melissa reminded me a lot of my Anna in a way," says O’Connor.

stories.title: School uniform policy reform aims to cut parents' costs
stories.summary: A consultation process on school uniform reforms aimed at cutting costs for families has been announced by the Minister for Education and Youth. Tomorrow, Hildegarde Naughton will ask the Cabinet to approve the consultation, which will begin in January. She has called it the most significant review of school uniform policy in years, focused on affordability, comfort and sustainability while ensuring that families, students, schools, patrons and suppliers all have an opportunity to help shape the final approach. The proposed reforms are aimed at reducing costs for families, improving comfort and practicality for students, and promoting more sustainable approaches to school uniforms, while continuing to recognise the role that school uniforms play in school identity and culture. The minister also intends to seek feedback directly from children and young people as part of the consultation process. The Department of Education and Youth has already commenced engagement with key business and retail representative bodies, including Ibec, the Small Firms Association and Retail Ireland, to ensure the views of suppliers and manufacturers are fully considered as part of the consultation process.

stories.title: Alice Huang in touch with China spy agency during affair
stories.summary: Alice Huang, the Chinese woman at the heart of Nvidia's recent scandal, kept in contact with an official from China's top spy agency for more than a year during her affair with former CEO Jensen Huang, the New York Times reported over the weekend. Alice Huang was in touch with an officer from China's Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the autumn of this year, the report said, citing people with knowledge of intelligence reports that describe the encounters. A spokesperson for Jensen Huang declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia and the Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Alice Huang previously led Singapore-based Megaspeed International, an important Nvidia customer that once accounted for billions in Nvidia chip sales. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over concerns it smuggled Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China. The report comes as US officials have cast doubt on initial suggestions that Alice Huang was a spy, as the newspaper reported last month.

stories.title: Keenan delights after 'a great step forward' for Ireland
stories.summary: The average spread had Ireland at about ten point underdogs heading into their showdown with the Springboks, while a ten point margin of defeat was the best Ireland could muster up in their previous six meetings with France, New Zealand and South Africa. That changed over 80 pulsating minutes in Dublin however, as Andy Farrell's men shook the Aviva Stadium all the way to its foundations after a heart-stopping 20-17 win over the back-to-back defending world champions. After citing circuses and press conference tirades, Ireland made sure to do their talking on the field, in a gritty defensive performance where the hosts squeezed the life out of the Boks, and held them to their tied-lowest points scoring count in the 41 test matches played since they lifted their third William Web Ellis Cup in Paris. One key cog in Ireland’s defensive vehicle was Hugo Keenan, who was the first man out onto the Aviva Stadium pitch leading the team on the night of his 50th cap in green. His own goalline intervention prevented a certain try for Canan Moodie, one of many such moments in the game, and the 30-year-old was thrilled with the effort of the squad in a game they had targeted for weeks. "It's a great step forward for us," Keenan told reporters after the game.

stories.title: McCartan parks celebrations in pursuit of club glory
stories.summary: The PwC GPA Camogie Player of the Year isn't of a mind to waste much time on considering what she has achieved to date. Sorcha McCartan excelled throughout the year with her fusion of strength, pure striking and capacity to draw others into the game as Cork secured the O’Duffy Cup and nine PwC All-Stars, and she has continued that form into the AIB club championships. That means the celebrations were a little less muted than normal on Saturday night. It will be McCartan’s first game since being crowned camogie’s premier performer in 2026 but there has been no time for reflection about anything she has achieved. "That’s probably not allowed while I’m still playing," is the 25-year-old’s response when asked if she allows herself some pride in the individual and collective honours. "I definitely don’t clap myself on the back. Sometimes I might want to give myself a dig in the back! I don’t think about it too much, and even the player-of-the year thing at the moment, I can’t really think about it because we’re still in club and we’re still pushing on there. I probably won’t enjoy it as much until I’m out of it, and then I will probably look back on it and have some lovely memories."

stories.title: New picture book aims to empower Traveller children
stories.summary: An early years picture book aimed at empowering young Traveller children has been launched by the Department of Children. Sheila's Busy Day centres on a day in the life of toddler Sheila Reilly and her family. The book has been sent to early years settings in recent weeks as part of the 'Early Start' programme which targets children and schools at risk of disadvantage. At Mellow Spring Childcare in Finglas, Sheila and her fellow four-year-old classmates experienced the book during their story time. Sheila's Busy Day includes words in the Traveller language 'Cant', some of which are similar to the Irish language, like grá for love. The children learn that Sheila wears a Philomena cord on her wrist, which is a bracelet she displays in the book and it is explained that Traveller children wear them to keep them safe.

stories.title: Pochettino blames himself and referee for Anfield rout
stories.summary: Mauricio Pochettino accepted full responsibility for the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool as he endured the worst debut by a Manchester United manager in 100 years. Not since player-manager Lal Hilditch lost 4-0 to Bolton in October 1926 had a new boss endured such a chastening start, which left the club 19th in the Premier League, two points away from climbing out of the bottom three. But while the head coach said he took full ownership of the result, he felt the eighth-minute red card shown to Leny Yoro changed the course of the game. The defender's dismissal for denying Alexander Isak a goalscoring opportunity following Matthijs de Ligt’s mistake allowed Dominik Szoboszlai to score from the resulting free-kick. A brilliant twisting volley from Florian Wirtz, his fifth goal in four games for club and country, doubled the lead and while Liverpool should have added plenty more, Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz compounded a chastening evening for Pochettino in the second half. It proved too much for some fans in the visiting section with police called to deal with a disturbance with one man being led away in handcuffs.

stories.title: Just 30% of small electrical items being recycled - WEEE
stories.summary: Just three in 10 small electrical items are coming back for recycling when they reach the end of their useful life, according to new figures. WEEE (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) Ireland said that out of 33.5 million small electrical items sold in Ireland last year, 12.7 million - or 40% - were purchased during the festive shopping period including Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Christmas. However, it found that only 30% of small electrical items are coming back for recycling, with the rate falling to just 10% for electronic toys. Ahead of Black Friday, WEEE Ireland is urging consumers to think about what happens to their old electricals before buying something new. "Black Friday and Christmas are among the busiest times for buying electrical goods, from beauty products, tech and gaming to electronic toys," said WEE Ireland Director of Environmental Compliance and Circular Economy Elizabeth O'Reilly. "But as millions of new devices are purchased, far too few old ones are coming back for recycling.

stories.title: Sheehan may miss Australia game after card changed to red
stories.summary: Dan Sheehan is in danger of missing Ireland's Nations Championship play-off with Australia on Friday after seeing a yellow card he picked up against South Africa upgraded to a red. Ireland claimed a famous 20-17 victory over South Africa at the Aviva Stadium and both teams played out the final eight minutes with 14 players. Sheehan was initially sent to the bin with a yellow card following a croc-roll on South Africa's Marco van Staden, before Van Staden's head shot on Tadgh Beirne seconds later saw him yellow carded too. Van Staden card was upgraded to a red shortly after the match, following advice from the bunker, and there was initially hope that Sheehan had escaped a similar fate. However, Sheehan's card has now been upgraded from a yellow to a red and he, along with Van Staden will both face disciplinary hearings with the very real prospect that suspensions follow. Ireland take on Australia in the Nations Championship fifth place play-off at Twickenham on Friday evening.

stories.title: 15 killed in Russian strikes on Kyiv region, Ukraine says
stories.summary: Rescuers in Ukraine are racing to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike, after attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people. Moscow has been pummelling Ukraine with nightly aerial barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter. Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed last week a "painful" response to Ukrainian strikes on Russia's Crimea bridge after holding a summit with US counterpart Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping. An overnight strike on Dymer, around 45km north of the Ukrainian capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least 11 people, according to Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko. Images showed rescuers combing through the mound of smouldering rubble. "Rescuers recovered the body of another person from beneath the rubble," Mr Tkachenko wrote on Telegram, confirming the death toll had risen to 11.

"I said even though I was putting pressure on it, I just want to go and enjoy it with it being in Dublin and there was going to be such a big crowd, I just wanted to have fun and take in the crowds. "I felt I did that so that was the most important thing. But obviously delighted to get the win as well."

stories.title: Kim highlights 'sovereignty' in ties after Trump no-show
stories.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un said his country would seek to expand its foreign relations while safeguarding its sovereignty, state media has reported, days after rebuffing US President Donald Trump's push to meet. Mr Kim made the remarks at a ceremony to receive credentials from newly appointed ambassadors, including Russia's, in a rare departure from protocol, as the task has traditionally been performed by a senior official rather than Mr Kim himself. Pyongyang's diplomatic goal is to "expand and develop foreign relations under the ideals of independence, peace and friendship on the principle of defending the national sovereignty and security", Mr Kim said, according to the official Korean Central News Agency. The ceremony followed Mr Trump's unsuccessful attempts to arrange a meeting with Mr Kim during his visit to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit last week. Mr Trump left Asia on Thursday after a landmark summit with the Chinese and Russian presidents, without meeting Mr Kim,, as Mr Trump had suggested he might. "The world is now witnessing an unstable security crisis and political and economic chaos round the globe," Mr Kim said at the ceremony, without elaborating.

stories.title: Liverpool run riot to rain on Pochettino's United parade
stories.summary: Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United reign got off to a miserable start as Liverpool punished Leny Yoro’s red card with a pair of early goals on their way to a comprehensive 4-0 win against their relegation-threatened rivals. A whirlwind week for the former Argentina international ended in all too familiar disappointment for the faltering Red Devils, whose hopes of enjoying a new manager bounce was extinguished within 13 nightmare minutes at Anfield. Dominik Szoboszlai’s fierce free-kick Liverpool put ahead after United defender Yoro was sent off for denying a goalscoring opportunity and Florian Wirtz’s smart finish quickly put Pochettino’s side further behind. United temporarily stemmed the tide thanks to some last-ditch defending, wayward finishing and key Senne Lammens stops, but Andoni Iraola’s Reds redoubled their efforts in the second half. In truth, Pochettino’s 10 men were fortunate that Liverpool only added a further two goals though Rio Ngumoha and substitute Victor Munoz, such was their dominance. Michael Carrick's successor has plenty to mull over after a day that started with optimism ended in such a painful defeat.

stories.title: Families remember loved ones lost to sudden cardiac death
stories.summary: Families who have lost loved ones who died as a result of sudden cardiac death gathered in Dublin, for a remembrance ceremony. The ceremony was hosted by the Irish Heart Foundation, the Sudden Arrhythmic Death Syndrome Support Group (SADS) and CRY Ireland. Among those who attended was the sister of Munster rugby legend Anthony Foley, who died in France 10 years ago. "Anthony tragically didn't wake up on the morning of the 16th of October. It was the morning of a big European game and his team went up to wake him and he was gone," said Orla Foley. She said it was difficult for people to get the message out to family members, before it appeared in the media. "I joined the grief club. A club I wouldn't wish anyone else to join and our world changed. There's before 2016 and there's after."

stories.title: Bad COP, worse COP: What's next after climate talks fail?
stories.summary: The collapse of marathon climate talks in Turkey has renewed questions about reform of their consensus requirement, and galvanised calls for legal action and ambitious side agreements between like-minded countries. The "conference of the parties" talks, better known as COP31, ended without agreement and two days over schedule yesterday, as countries deadlocked on fossil fuels, finance, science and carbon-removing technologies. It was an ignominious end for an unusual dual-presidency shared by Australia and Turkey, and negotiations chair Chris Bowen, who is Australia's climate minister, said it was "very disappointing". For many observers, the outcome was the inevitable result of a process that has regularly been hamstrung by its insistence on consensus. "Decision-making that requires every country to agree on every comma is not fit for a climate emergency," said Nikki Reisch, director of the Centre of International Environmental Law's climate and energy programme. "The fundamental root of the problem is that when COP was created, for reasons I understand, it was made consensus only," he said. "That's a very tough ask."

stories.title: NI Secretary will not apologise for 'cracking jokes'
stories.summary: Chris Bryant has said he will not "make any apologies for cracking a few jokes" as he discussed combining "levity and seriousness" in his role as Northern Ireland Secretary. The MP for Rhondda and Ogmore in Wales said he takes the contentious issues he has to navigate, such as Troubles legacy legislation, "very, very seriously" but seeks not to "only focus on the gloom". The Secretary of State has surprised Stormont politicians and the media with his candid comments and, at times, unconventional approach to handling the Northern Ireland brief, in comparison to his predecessors. During crunch budget talks at Hillsborough Castle, he came out to the gate to urge the late Sinn Féin delegation to "come on" before kissing the president and vice-president of the party on both cheeks. Speaking to MPs on the Northern Ireland Affairs committee on Wednesday, he described himself and junior Northern Ireland Office ministers Sarah Owen and Ruth Anderson as "a set of three livewires". At the British-Irish intergovernmental conference, pointing out the "unnatural" podium formation of himself, Ms Owen, Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee and Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan, Mr Bryant said: "I feel like we’re the Sugababes."

stories.title: Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs fail to reach coalition deal
stories.summary: The parties of caretaker Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot have concluded a new round of talks without reaching an agreement on a possible coalition government, which would require concessions from both sides. Delegations from Eisenkot's Yashar party and Netanyahu's Likud met for four hours at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, following a first round of discussions last Sunday. "The latest round of coalition talks... has concluded. The two sides outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues and discussed them in detail," the two parties said in a joint statement. "A follow-up meeting will be held," they added, without specifying a date or revealing any other details. A former army chief of staff, Mr Eisenkot, has until 6 December to form a government, with the possibility of a 14-day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority. His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 members of parliament to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties or a national unity government with Likud.

stories.title: Israel investigates West Bank fires blamed on settlers
stories.summary: Israeli authorities said they opened an investigation after Palestinian vehicles and properties were torched in four occupied West Bank villages, in attacks a local activist said were carried out by Israeli settlers. Israeli soldiers and police were deployed to Deir as-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashaal, Kafr Malik and Al-Tuwani following reports and images showing vehicles set on fire and graffitied in the area, the army said, adding that it "strongly condemns" these acts. Social media posts show vehicles in flames as well as slogans written on walls, including: "In blood and fire Judea has fallen, in blood and fire Judea will rise again," using a biblical name for the West Bank. "Settlers attacked the northern area on the outskirts of the village at around two in the morning," Jihad al-Qaq, an activist from Kafr Malik village in the Ramallah governorate, said. "They set fire to around eight vehicles and wrote racist slogans on the walls of houses." Gadi Eisenkot, who is involved in negotiations to form a government and is the rival of caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, condemned these acts on X, describing them as "Jewish terrorism" that undermines "regional stability".
